(a) In General.—Section 43(c)(6) of the Act entitled “An Act to provide for the registration and protection of trademarks used in commerce, to carry out the provisions of certain international conventions, and for other purposes”, approved July 5, 1946 (commonly referred to as the “Trademark Act of 1946”; 15 U.S.C. 1125(c)(6)), is amended by striking subparagraphs (A) and (B) and inserting the following:“(A) is brought by another person under the common law or a statute of a State; and“(B)(i) seeks to prevent dilution by blurring or dilution by tarnishment; or“(ii) asserts any claim of actual or likely damage or harm to the distinctiveness or reputation of a mark, label, or form of advertisement.”. 
    (b) Effective Date.—The amendment made by subsection (a) shall apply to any action commenced on or after the date of the enactment of this Act.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the references to an "action" and claims "brought by another person" grant a right to sue. That fails because these are private trademark dilution suits between private parties under state law, and the amendment only defines when federal registration bars such claims. It does not grant any outside party a right to sue over or object to a federal decision, and it provides for no consultation, comment period, hearing, rulemaking, or advisory body.
fable.s: is brought by another person under the common law or a statute of a State

opus.w: This amendment sets out which private state-law dilution claims a federal trademark registration blocks. It is about lawsuits between private parties, not a right to sue the government over a federal decision. Mentioning an action 'brought by another person' is tempting, but describing or limiting private litigation is not the same as granting an outside party the right to challenge a federal decision. No consultation, hearing, comment period or advisory body is involved.
opus.s: “(A) is brought by another person under the common law or a statute of a State; and“(B)(i) seeks to prevent dilution by blurring or dilution by tarnishment
opus.b: I'd label this **No**. The tempting reading is that "an action... brought by another person" grants an outside party a right to sue. It doesn't. This provision changes when a federal trademark registration blocks a private claim brought under state law between private parties. It limits that litigation rather than letting anyone challenge a federal decision, and nothing in it involves consultation, hearings, comment periods or advisory bodies.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the Trademark Act to define the scope of state law claims for trademark dilution. It does not require the federal government to consult with outside parties before making a decision, nor does it grant a right to sue the federal government over a specific agency decision. It merely clarifies the legal standards for private litigation between non-federal parties or under state law, which falls outside the definition of participation in federal decision-making.
qwen_chat.s: (a) In General.—Section 43(c)(6) of the Act entitled “An Act to provide for the registration and protection of trademarks used in commerce, to carry out the provisions of certain international conventions, and for other purposes”, approved July 5, 1946 (commonly referred to as the “Trademark Act of 1946”; 15 U.S.C. 1125(c)(6)), is amended by striking subparagraphs (A) and (B) and inserting the following:“(A) is brought by another person under the common law or a statute of a State; and“(B)(i) seeks to prevent dilution by blurring or dilution by tarnishment; or“(ii) asserts any claim of actual or likely damage or harm to the distinctiveness or reputation of a mark, label, or form of advertisement.”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the text amends a statute regarding legal actions ("brought by another person"), it involves participation in the sense of litigation. However, the definition explicitly states that "a court's jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits - limiting or describing litigation is not the same as GRANTING an outside party a right to sue a decision." This section merely defines the scope of existing common law or state statutory claims for trademark dilution; it does not create a new federal decision-making process that requires consultation with outsiders, nor does it grant a new right to sue the federal government. It is a substantive amendment to trademark law, not a procedural requirement for public participation in federal agency decisions.
